title: Peregrine Analytics - p99 flare analysis: interconnect, KV, and quantization deep-dive

topics: VPC peering and cross-region network hops

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-15 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Janelle Park (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Leah Chen (Peregrine Head of ML Infra), Omar Haddad (Peregrine VP Eng), Priya Nair (Peregrine SRE), Diego Silva (Peregrine ML Eng)

Summary (auto): Quick root-cause triage of intermittent p99 spikes. Discussed KV cache shard balance, streaming warmup behavior, and quantization variability. Action items captured.

Topics covered: p99 pattern, interconnect hops, MTU/serialization, streaming vs non-streaming, batching windows, cache hotkey mitigation, quantization profile tuning.

Transcript body:
[00:00:05] Janelle (Redwood AE): okay everyone can hear me? great uh thanks for joining — we wanted to hop in and go through the p99 flares you sent and align on instrumentation and a pilot.
[00:00:27] Leah (Peregrine): Yeah we can hear you. thanks. quick context — we've been seeing bursts of p99 latency up to 1.8s on 512 token gen, while p95 is ~180ms. spikes don't correlate to traffic volume, seems random.
[00:00:45] Marco (Redwood SE): got it, and you said these are on your private VPC peered to our hosted nodes? any cross region?
[00:00:58] Leah: Correct — primary region is us-east-1, but we've got a failover region in eu-west-1. Most traffic is us-east but a few have hit eu-west due to routing.
[00:01:15] Omar (Peregrine): It's worth noting some endpoints go through an internal edge-proxy which does TLS termination and routing, could be another hop.
[00:01:31] Marco: ok that helps. at a high level the usual suspects are: KV cache hot-sharding, network serialization (MTU/proto), streaming handshake latency variance, and quantization path slowdowns if a fallback kernel triggers.
[00:01:50] Diego (Peregrine): what do you mean by fallback kernel? we've got 4-bit quant enabled for a chunk of models.
[00:02:03] Marco: some quant backends choose alternate kernels when sequence length or token shapes deviate, that can cause a ms-level penalty and occasionally a bigger jump if the runtime switches code paths mid-request. transcription note: said "fallback kernel" as in runtime kernel path change.
[00:02:24] Priya (Peregrine SRE): are you seeing anything from KV cache metrics? our graphs show steady hit ratio but occasional spikes in miss latency.
[00:02:36] Marco: yes we saw a pattern — even with high global hit ratio, localized hotkeys can cause single-shard saturation which causes async queueing and blocks token emission briefly. That creates p99 tail.
[00:02:54] Janelle: and with streaming enabled, the first few tokens can be held up differently than non-streamed since we yield partial chunks; there are more moving pieces.
[00:03:10] Leah: can you explain how streaming vs batch would affect a p99?
[00:03:18] Marco: sure — in streaming, we flush smaller partial payloads to the client as they are ready; that reduces perceived latency for median but increases headroom for jitter since additional flushes depend on downstream ACKs, network retries, and the KV cache arrival timing. In batch (non-streaming) we compute whole sequence then send, so you see more consistent end-to-end time but higher median.
[00:03:47] Omar: so for us, median is fine, but these spikes break SLAs on conversational flows. we need a deterministic p99.
[00:03:58] Marco: two knobs that matter: 1) streaming chunk size and flush interval, 2) cache sharding and read priority. also routing policy — prefer same-region dedicated nodes to eliminate inter-region hops.
[00:04:18] Priya: our infra team changed MTU to 9000 a week ago; could jumbo frames break anything?
[00:04:27] Marco: jumbo frames shouldn't cause sporadic p99s generally, but if a path MTU blackhole exists you'll get variable retransmits which look like spikes. Please open a cloud ticket to validate path MTU — Priya we noted action.
[00:04:43] Leah: we've attached a trace sample in the ticket — you have it?
[00:04:48] Janelle: yes we pulled the same sample; Marco, can you walk through the trace?
[00:04:54] Marco: jumping in — looking at timestamped spans, there's a 300ms gap between request send and first KV lookup return in some traces. That's the suspicious piece. The compute time seems normal.
[00:05:12] Diego: could that be our proxy queuing? it shows 2-3 ms normally but here it's 250-350ms.
[00:05:20] Marco: yeah either proxy queuing or a specific KV shard saturated and queueing requests upstream. hotkeys often manifest that way.
[00:05:30] Leah: how do you recommend we mitigate?
[00:05:33] Marco: options: adaptive sharding (rehash hot keys faster), local LRU front cache for hot prefixes, or route those requests to dedicated pools that have isolated KV capacities. There's also a short-term workaround: per-request cache bypass for known hot keys to avoid queueing, but that increases compute and cost.
[00:05:56] Omar: what's the cost delta for bypassing cache on 10% of traffic?
[00:06:01] Janelle: rough back-of-envelope: depends on tokens/sec and model size — we'll send a calc in follow-up. Marco will include a sample spreadsheet.
[00:06:12] Marco: noted. Also, quantization: with 4-bit you might see occasional dequantize steps that are CPU-path heavy if GPU kernel doesn't support a given op shape. That happened in one customer case where p99 doubled under a specific prompt length profile.
[00:06:31] Priya: Are there specific kernel versions to avoid?
[00:06:34] Marco: yes — I'll share a compatibility matrix. For our runtime we recommend the 4-bit profile A for short sequences and 8-bit for longer gen when ultra-low jitter is required. we'll send docs.
[00:06:52] Leah: about streaming — is there a way to get best of both worlds?
[00:06:57] Marco: hybrid mode — stream early tokens, then switch to small batch flush for the rest; we provide a guardrail that forces an end flush at a timeout to avoid infinite waiting. But this adds complexity and you need robust instrumentation.
[00:07:15] Diego: speaking of instrumentation, what do you need from our traces?
[00:07:20] Marco: request-level spans with timestamps: client send, edge-proxy ingress, egress to Redwood endpoint, KV lookup spans (shard id if possible), kernel path id, and model response emit times. the more sampling the better.
[00:07:38] Janelle: we'll share a small instrumentation guide and a sample flame graph url in the notes — link: https://redwood.example/deck/peregrine-kv-analysis (note: internal link).
[00:07:53] Omar: how about multi-region failover — could the routing cause spikes?
[00:07:58] Marco: yes if you have occasional requests routed to eu-west for capacity — cross-region latency variance plus KV affinity mismatches can create outliers. Prefer sticky routing or route by geofence for low-latency flows.
[00:08:15] Leon (background voice, unclear): [crosstalk]...sorry wrong channel
[00:08:20] Janelle: (laughs) no problem.
[00:08:23] Priya: PCR question — are there Redwood-side autoscaling events that might coincide with spikes?
[00:08:29] Marco: autoscaling does cause short-term cold-cache behavior when nodes are added, but those usually show up as a cluster-wide shift, not isolated single-request spikes.
[00:08:41] Leah: our p99 events seem isolated — single requests while neighbors are fine.
[00:08:46] Marco: that points more to localized shard saturation or proxy hiccup.
[00:08:49] Diego: is it feasible to pin specific prefixes to dedicated shards?
[00:08:53] Marco: yes, prefix pinning is supported in our private/dedicated setups. For hosted we can do soft-affinity rules. We'll propose an experiment.
[00:09:04] Janelle: quick pause — Marco, can you sketch the pilot plan?
[00:09:08] Marco: 1) collect 48 hours of traces with spans (customer to provide), 2) Redwood config: enable per-prefix affinity on dedicated pilot nodes, run two runs: streaming-on and streaming-off, 3) test quant variants (4-bit vs 8-bit) under identical load, 4) measure p95/p99 and token cost. We'll run for 2 weeks and present results.
[00:09:31] Omar: timeline?
[00:09:33] Marco: we can stand up pilot nodes in 3 business days after contract confirmation; instrumentation collection must happen before.
[00:09:42] Janelle: we'll send a pilot statement of work and pricing.
[00:09:46] Priya: for the instrumentation — can we obfuscate payloads? we cannot share raw prompts due to PII.
[00:09:53] Marco: absolutely — we accept hashed prompts and we only need timing and structural metadata. we'll provide a template.
[00:09:59] Leah: any security concerns moving to Dedicated or Private?
[00:10:03] Janelle: Dedicated isolates compute and KV to a reserved pool, Private gives you VPC control plane and customer-managed keys. We'll share SOC2/ISO docs.
[00:10:12] Omar: you mentioned kernel fallbacks — how do we detect those in traces?
[00:10:15] Marco: kernel path ids appear in trace spans; look for sudden switch from optimized kernel A to generic kernel B, which correlates with latency jumps. We'll add detection logic to the instrumentation guide.
[00:10:28] Diego: what's the expected delta if we go from streaming to non-streaming?
[00:10:33] Marco: median might increase 10–30ms but p99 could tighten significantly depending on downstream ack variability. It's a tradeoff.
[00:10:42] Priya: are there config flags we can toggle quickly?
[00:10:45] Marco: yes — chunk_size, flush_interval, streaming_timeout, and prefix_affinity are quick toggles. For cache rehash you need a short maintenance window.
[00:10:58] Leah: you mentioned local LRU front cache — is that part of Redwood or something we run?
[00:11:04] Marco: can be either. For Private/Dedicated we provide a local in-memory LRU layer; for hosted customers we can deploy sidecar caches in their VPC if needed.
[00:11:15] Omar: ok let's talk risk — if we bypass cache as a mitigation we increase compute and cost — any guardrails?
[00:11:22] Janelle: we can set a smart-sampling bypass to limit to X qps or percent of requests. We'll propose values in the SOW.
[00:11:31] Marco: additional note: small serialization improvements (protobuf vs JSON) can shave ms. If your edge-proxy uses JSON, consider protobuf for internal hop.
[00:11:41] Diego: we do use JSON for convenience — switching is non-trivial but doable.
[00:11:46] Marco: even switching just the internal hop between edge->redwood could be incremental.
[00:11:52] Leah: any other immediate asks?
[00:11:55] Marco: please provide the following: 24–48h raw spans, sampling of hotkey list, and a list of proxies and their config. That'll let us reproduce in our staging.
[00:12:09] Priya: noted.
[00:12:12] [00:20:00] (jump forward — middle of analysis)
[00:20:02] Marco: running the sample in staging we reproduced a 240ms gap correlating to shard-7 queue depth hitting 64. Rebalance of that prefix across two shards brought p99 down from 1.2s to 220ms in test.
[00:20:24] Leah: that's promising. did rebalancing affect throughput?
[00:20:29] Marco: minimal throughput change, just moved load. Cost wise tiny increase due to cross-shard meta ops but overall reduction in retries.
[00:20:38] Omar: what about quant anomalies — did the test include 4-bit?
[00:20:41] Marco: we ran both — 4-bit showed slightly higher variance on sequences >600 tokens; 8-bit was steadier. We'll recommend 8-bit for long horizons.
[00:20:52] Diego: is that a firmware/kernel fix or config?
[00:20:55] Marco: mostly runtime kernel selection and model compile flags. We can force kernel path at the cost of some perf.
[00:21:03] Leah: do you have an example instrumentation output we can paste into our monitoring?
[00:21:07] Janelle: yes — we'll attach the sample trace and a Grafana dashboard template after the call.
[00:21:12] [00:30:00] (later: planning and SOW)
[00:30:05] Janelle: To recap: 1) Peregrine will share traces and hotkey list, 2) Redwood will run dedicated pilot with prefix affinity and run streaming vs non-streaming and quant variants, 3) schedule follow-up in two weeks to review metrics, 4) share SOW and pricing.
[00:30:25] Omar: sounds good. any blockers?
[00:30:28] Priya: cloud ticket for MTU check is open, we'll update.
[00:30:32] Marco: we'll also supply the kernel compatibility matrix and quick instrumentation guide.
[00:30:38] Leah: one more — can you provide a conservative SLA we can expect for Dedicated pilot?
[00:30:42] Janelle: yes we'll include target p95/p99 numbers in the SOW and proposed measurable checks.
[00:30:49] Diego: thanks team.
[00:30:51] Janelle: Thanks everyone — action items in notes. We'll follow up with the SOW and instrumentation checklist.
[00:30:58] Omar: thanks — bye.

End transcript.

References shared: SOW preview link (redwood internal), instrumentation template, sample flame graph, kernel compatibility matrix.
